claim: Functional compensation is a common notion in the neuroscience of healthy ageing, whereby older adults are proposed to recruit additional brain activity to compensate for reduced cognitive function.
source: Functional compensation is a common notion in the neuroscience of healthy ageing, whereby older adults are proposed to recruit additional brain activity to compensate for reduced cognitive function.
evidence: This is a statement about the concept of functional compensation in the field, drawing on established scientific understanding.

claim: Whether additional brain activity in older participants actually helps their cognitive performance remains debated.
source: However, whether this additional brain activity in older participants actually helps their cognitive performance remains debated.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of scientific debate in the field.

claim: The study examined brain activity and cognitive performance in a human lifespan sample of N = 223 participants.
source: We examined brain activity and cognitive performance in a human lifespan sample (N = 223) while they performed a problem-solving task (based on Cattell's test of fluid intelligence) during functional magnetic resonance imaging.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size of the study.

claim: Activity in bilateral cuneal cortex for hard vs. easy problems increased both with age and with performance.
source: Whole-brain univariate analysis revealed that activity in bilateral cuneal cortex for hard vs. easy problems increased both with age and with performance, even when adjusting for an estimate of age-related differences in cerebrovascular reactivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-brain univariate analysis.

claim: The age and performance effects in bilateral cuneal cortex remained even when adjusting for an estimate of age-related differences in cerebrovascular reactivity.
source: Whole-brain univariate analysis revealed that activity in bilateral cuneal cortex for hard vs. easy problems increased both with age and with performance, even when adjusting for an estimate of age-related differences in cerebrovascular reactivity.
evidence: This describes a control analysis adjusting for vascular effects.

claim: Age increased the likelihood that activation patterns in the cuneal region provided non-redundant information about the two task conditions, beyond that of the multiple demand network.
source: Multivariate Bayesian decoding further demonstrated that age increased the likelihood that activation patterns in this cuneal region provided non-redundant information about the two task conditions, beyond that of the multiple demand network generally activated in this task.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the multivariate Bayesian decoding analysis.

claim: The findings constitute some of the strongest evidence yet for functional compensation in healthy ageing, at least in the cuneal region during visual problem-solving.
source: This constitutes some of the strongest evidence yet for functional compensation in healthy ageing, at least in this brain region during visual problem-solving.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the data presented and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Preventing cognitive decline in old age is a major public health priority.
source: Preventing cognitive decline in old age is a major public heath priority, which demands a better understanding of the neurophysiological changes that preserve cognitive function despite progressive brain atrophy (Cabeza et al., 2018; Christensen et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neuroimaging has facilitated the idea that the brain can flexibly respond to tissue loss by recruiting additional brain activity to support cognitive functions.
source: Neuroimaging has facilitated the idea that the brain can flexibly respond to tissue loss (e.g., due to ageing) by recruiting additional brain activity to support cognitive functions (Cabeza et al., 2018; Grady, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: If additional recruitment in older adults improves their behavioural performance, this reorganisation of brain function constitutes a functional compensation mechanism.
source: If this additional recruitment in older adults improves their behavioural performance, it is argued that this reorganisation of brain function constitutes a functional compensation mechanism (Cabeza, 2002).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Fluid intelligence shows one of the most consistent and largest decreases in older age.
source: Fluid intelligence (i.e., solving novel abstract problems) is a cognitive function that shows one of the most consistent and largest decreases in older age (Salthouse et al., 2008; Deary, 2012; Ghisletta et al., 2012; Kievit et al., 2014; Bors and Forrin, 1995; Salthouse and Pink, 2008; Schretlen et al., 2000; Clay et al., 2009; Kievit et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Fluid intelligence tasks engage the multiple demand network (MDN), which comprises lateral prefrontal, posterior parietal, and cingulate regions.
source: Functional (Duncan and Owen, 2000; Gray et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2006; Crittenden et al., 2016; Tschentscher et al., 2017) and structural (Colom et al., 2009; Jauk et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2020; Paul et al., 2016; Zamroziewicz et al., 2018) neuroimaging has shown that fluid intelligence tasks engage the multiple demand network (MDN; Duncan, 2010), which comprises lateral prefrontal, posterior parietal, and cingulate regions.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior functional and structural neuroimaging studies.

claim: MDN activation tends to decrease with age as measured with fMRI during problem-solving tasks that tax fluid intelligence such as the Cattell task.
source: MDN activation tends to decrease with age as measured, for example, with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) during problem-solving tasks that tax fluid intelligence such as the Cattell task (Samu et al., 2017; Mitchell et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Previous studies have examined age effects in core regions of the MDN but have not explicitly tested for functional compensation in other regions.
source: So far, these studies have examined age effects in core regions of the MDN but have not explicitly tested for functional compensation in other regions.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior research.

claim: The study conducted a whole-brain voxel-wise search for clusters that showed a positive relationship with both age and cognitive performance.
source: To search for brain regions that might support functional compensation, we conducted a whole-brain voxel-wise search for clusters that showed a positive relationship with both age and cognitive performance (i.e., classic univariate criteria for functional compensation; Lövdén et al., 2010; Cabeza et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The dependent variable was the difference in fMRI activation for blocks of hard vs. easy odd-one-out problems.
source: The dependent variable was the difference in fMRI activation for blocks of hard vs. easy odd-one-out problems (Figure 1A), as measured in 223 adults between 19 and 87 years of age, from Stage 3 of the Cambridge Centre for Ageing & Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) project (Shafto et al., 2014); performance was measured as the proportion of all problems correct.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and measures.

claim: Performance was measured as the proportion of all problems correct.
source: The dependent variable was the difference in fMRI activation for blocks of hard vs. easy odd-one-out problems (Figure 1A), as measured in 223 adults between 19 and 87 years of age, from Stage 3 of the Cambridge Centre for Ageing & Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) project (Shafto et al., 2014); performance was measured as the proportion of all problems correct.
evidence: This describes the behavioral performance measure.

claim: The study applied a multivariate Bayesian (MVB) approach across all voxels within candidate regions to test whether multi-voxel patterns provided additional information about task difficulty, beyond that in the MDN.
source: Second, we applied a multivariate Bayesian (MVB) approach (Friston et al., 2008) across all voxels within any candidate regions identified in the whole-brain search, to test whether multi-voxel patterns in these regions provided additional information about task difficulty, beyond that in the MDN.
evidence: This describes the multivariate analysis method used.

claim: If a region were involved in functional compensation, the additional information it contains about the task would increase with age.
source: We predicted that, if a region were involved in functional compensation, the additional information it contains about the task would increase with age.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the compensation hypothesis.

claim: The cuneus showed evidence of additional multivariate information, supporting its role in functional compensation.
source: To pre-empt the results, unlike in our previous applications of MVB (Morcom and Henson, 2018; Knights et al., 2021), we find one region – within the cuneus – that did show evidence of this additional multivariate information, supporting its role in functional compensation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Behavioural performance decreased with age during the fMRI scan on the modified version of the Cattell task.
source: As expected from prior studies, behavioural performance decreased with age during the fMRI scan on the modified version of the Cattell task (collapsed across hard and easy conditions; see Methods) (standardised coefficient = −5.65, t(220) = −14, p < 0.001, R2 = 0.48; Figure 1B, upper).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding with statistical support and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: There was a high correlation (r = 0.79, p < 0.001) between performance measures from the fMRI version and standard version of the Cattell task.
source: There was a high correlation between performance measures from the fMRI version and standard version of the Cattell task when the same people performed the standard Cattell task outside the scanner 1–3 years previously (r = 0.79, p < 0.001; Figure 1B, lower), suggesting that the version modified for fMRI was capturing the same cognitive ability.
evidence: This is a validation finding with statistical support and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The version of the Cattell task modified for fMRI was capturing the same cognitive ability as the standard version.
source: There was a high correlation between performance measures from the fMRI version and standard version of the Cattell task when the same people performed the standard Cattell task outside the scanner 1–3 years previously (r = 0.79, p < 0.001; Figure 1B, lower), suggesting that the version modified for fMRI was capturing the same cognitive ability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high correlation between the two versions.

claim: The [Hard > Easy] contrast showed bilateral activation across regions comprising the MDN, including the inferior/middle frontal gyri, intraparietal sulcus, anterior insula, and anterior cingulate cortex.
source: The [Hard > Easy] contrast showed bilateral activation across regions generally described as comprising the MDN (e.g., Duncan, 2010; Smith et al., 2021), including the inferior/middle frontal gyri, intraparietal sulcus, anterior insula, and anterior cingulate cortex (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding with reference to Figure 1C and citations to prior work defining the MDN.

claim: Additional activation was observed bilaterally in the inferior/ventral and lateral occipital temporal cortex, likely due to the visual nature of the task.
source: Additional activation was observed bilaterally in the inferior/ventral and lateral occipital temporal cortex (i.e., a cluster around the lateral occipital sulcus that extended anteriorly beyond the anterior occipital sulcus), likely due to the visual nature of the task.
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding with an interpretation based on task characteristics.

claim: Age-related increases in activity were widespread, including the precuneus, middle frontal gyrus, and supplementary motor area.
source: As reported using related measures and overlapping samples of Cam-CAN participants (Samu et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2023; Mitchell et al., 2023), age-related increases in activity were widespread, including the precuneus, middle frontal gyrus, and supplementary motor area.
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Activity positively related to performance was found in many of the same regions that were more active for hard vs. easy problems, including inferior/middle frontal gyrus, anterior cingulate, and superior parietal lobule.
source: Activity positively related to performance was found in many of the same regions that were more active for hard vs. easy problems (i.e., inferior/middle frontal gyrus, anterior cingulate, superior parietal lobule; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Two areas of the brain showed spatially overlapping positive effects of age and performance: bilateral cuneal cortex and bilateral frontal cortex.
source: Crucially, two areas of the brain showed spatially overlapping positive effects of age and performance, which is suggestive of an age-related compensatory response (Figure 2A, yellow intersection). These were in bilateral cuneal cortex (Figure 2B, magenta) and bilateral frontal cortex (Figure 2B, brown), the latter incorporating parts of the middle frontal gyri and anterior cingulate.
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding with reference to Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The overlapping positive effects of age and performance in bilateral cuneal cortex and bilateral frontal cortex are suggestive of an age-related compensatory response.
source: Crucially, two areas of the brain showed spatially overlapping positive effects of age and performance, which is suggestive of an age-related compensatory response (Figure 2A, yellow intersection).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neuroimaging findings.

claim: Based on traditional univariate analyses, bilateral cuneal cortex and bilateral frontal cortex are two candidate regions for age-related functional compensation.
source: Therefore, based on traditional univariate analyses, these are two candidate regions for age-related functional compensation (Cabeza and Dennis, 2013; Cabeza et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data and citations to prior work defining criteria for compensation.

claim: The frontal region showed additive effects of both age and performance.
source: However, the two candidate compensation regions showed different patterns as a function of age and performance: whereas the frontal region showed additive effects of both variables (Figure 2C, upper), the cuneus region showed signs of an interaction (p = 0.028; though this would not survive correction for multiple comparisons across the two ROIs), whereby the relationship with performance was strongest in the oldest participants (and there was little sign of a performance relationship in the youngest participants; Figure 2C, lower).
evidence: This is a statistical finding with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The cuneus region showed signs of an interaction (p = 0.028) between age and performance, whereby the relationship with performance was strongest in the oldest participants.
source: However, the two candidate compensation regions showed different patterns as a function of age and performance: whereas the frontal region showed additive effects of both variables (Figure 2C, upper), the cuneus region showed signs of an interaction (p = 0.028; though this would not survive correction for multiple comparisons across the two ROIs), whereby the relationship with performance was strongest in the oldest participants (and there was little sign of a performance relationship in the youngest participants; Figure 2C, lower).
evidence: This is a statistical finding with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The interaction in the cuneus region would not survive correction for multiple comparisons across the two ROIs.
source: However, the two candidate compensation regions showed different patterns as a function of age and performance: whereas the frontal region showed additive effects of both variables (Figure 2C, upper), the cuneus region showed signs of an interaction (p = 0.028; though this would not survive correction for multiple comparisons across the two ROIs), whereby the relationship with performance was strongest in the oldest participants (and there was little sign of a performance relationship in the youngest participants; Figure 2C, lower).
evidence: This is a statistical caveat about the interaction finding.

claim: The interaction pattern in the cuneus is suggestive of compensatory activation only engaged by higher-performing older people.
source: This is suggestive of compensatory activation only engaged by higher-performing older people in the cuneus specifically.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the interaction pattern.

claim: Many effects of age on the BOLD signal measured by fMRI relate to vascular effects of ageing, rather than necessarily indicating differences in neural activity.
source: It has previously been shown that many effects of age on the blood oxygenation level-dependent(BOLD) signal measured by fMRI relate to vascular effects of ageing, rather than necessarily indicating differences in neural activity (Tsvetanov et al., 2021a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: RSFA relates to age-related vascular differences.
source: Previous work has shown that RSFA relates to age-related vascular differences (Tsvetanov et al., 2021a), but not neural differences (Tsvetanov et al., 2015; Kumral et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RSFA does not relate to neural differences.
source: Previous work has shown that RSFA relates to age-related vascular differences (Tsvetanov et al., 2021a), but not neural differences (Tsvetanov et al., 2015; Kumral et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The pattern of effects remained similar in each ROI after RSFA adjustment.
source: Despite this RSFA adjustment, the pattern of effects remained similar in each ROI (Table 1; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the RSFA-adjusted analysis with reference to Table 1 and Figure 2C.

claim: The effects of age and the relationship with performance in both ROIs are neural in origin.
source: This suggests that these effects of age (and the relationship with performance) are neural in origin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RSFA-adjusted analysis.

claim: This check for vascular effects has not been performed in previous fMRI studies of age-related compensation.
source: This check has not been performed in previous fMRI studies of age-related compensation, which could reflect vascular effects of ageing instead.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the methodological approach.

claim: Previous fMRI studies of age-related compensation could reflect vascular effects of ageing instead of neural effects.
source: This check has not been performed in previous fMRI studies of age-related compensation, which could reflect vascular effects of ageing instead.
evidence: This is a speculation about the interpretation of prior studies.

claim: Across both joint models (MDN plus cuneal or frontal cortex), evidence of above-chance decoding was found for all except two participants.
source: Across both joint models (MDN plus cuneal or frontal cortex), we found evidence of above-chance decoding (real vs. shuffled log-evidence difference >3; see Methods) for all except two participants.
evidence: This is a finding from the MVB decoding analysis.

claim: Two participants (one of whom was the same across models) were removed from the MVB analysis.
source: These participants (the two points below the y = 3 dashed line in Figure 3A, one of whom was the same across models) were removed (Morcom and Henson, 2018; Knights et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for the MVB analysis with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: There was a significant positive effect of age on the likelihood that model performance was boosted by including voxel activation patterns from the cuneal ROI.
source: In line with this compensation account, there was a significant positive effect of age (Table 2) on the likelihood that model performance was boosted (i.e., log-evidence change >3) by including voxel activation patterns from the cuneal ROI (Figure 3B, lower; odds ratio = 2.21).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MVB boost analysis with reference to Table 2 and Figure 3B.

claim: The amount of unique task information in the multi-voxel pattern within the cuneal ROI (above that present in the MDN) increased with age.
source: In other words, the amount of unique task information in the multi-voxel pattern within the cuneal ROI (above that present in the MDN) increased with age.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MVB boost finding.

claim: The model containing the frontal ROI voxel activation patterns showed no effect of age on boost likelihood.
source: In contrast, this analysis for the model containing the frontal ROI voxel activation patterns showed no effect of age (Table 2; Figure 3B, upper).
evidence: This is a finding from the MVB boost analysis with reference to Table 2 and Figure 3B.

claim: The effect of age on boost likelihood in the cuneus is unlikely to be due to differences in the overall signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) across ages.
source: Note that, since this age effect in the cuneus was present even though the logistic regression model contained this ROI's univariate response as a covariate of no interest (Table 2), the effect of age on boost likelihood is unlikely to be due to differences in the overall signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) across ages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical model controlling for univariate response.

claim: There was no effect of age on the spread of weights for the cuneal cortex.
source: In this case, the results of this test did not support functional compensation, as there was no effect detected for the cuneal cortex and even a negative effect of age for the frontal cortex where the spread of the information across voxels was lower for older age (Figure 3C; Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the MVB spread analysis with reference to Figure 3C and Table 2.

claim: There was a negative effect of age for the frontal cortex where the spread of the information across voxels was lower for older age.
source: In this case, the results of this test did not support functional compensation, as there was no effect detected for the cuneal cortex and even a negative effect of age for the frontal cortex where the spread of the information across voxels was lower for older age (Figure 3C; Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the MVB spread analysis with reference to Figure 3C and Table 2.

claim: Even if an ROI were to have shown an effect of age on the spread measure, it could be explained by a non-specific mechanism that recruits multiple regions in tandem rather than reflecting compensation.
source: This said, it is worth highlighting that even if an ROI were to have shown an effect of age on this spread measure, it could instead be explained by a non-specific mechanism that recruits multiple regions in tandem (rather than reflecting compensation) as seen previously (Knights et al., 2021; also see Morcom and Johnson, 2015).
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the spread measure, supported by citations.

claim: The study identified two brain regions (in bilateral cuneal and frontal cortex) that satisfied traditional univariate criteria for functional compensation.
source: Here, we analysed fMRI data from a problem-solving (fluid intelligence) task and identified two brain regions (in bilateral cuneal and frontal cortex; Figure 2A, B) that satisfied traditional univariate criteria for functional compensation.
evidence: This is a summary of the univariate findings with reference to Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: After applying the multivariate criterion, only the cuneal cortex showed an age-related increase in additional information beyond that available in the MDN.
source: After applying the multivariate criterion that a compensating region should possess additional information about the task, only the cuneal cortex showed an age-related increase in this additional information (Figure 3B), beyond that available in the generic task-activated regions (i.e., the MDN; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a summary of the multivariate findings with reference to Figure 3B and Figure 1C.

claim: This is the first demonstration of increased multivariate information with age.
source: This is the first demonstration of increased multivariate information with age, since previous studies have shown evidence for no such multivariate increase associated with univariate age-related hyper-activation in other ROIs and tasks; leading to previous findings being interpreted in terms of neural inefficiency, rather than compensation (Morcom and Henson, 2018; Knights et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous studies have shown evidence for no multivariate increase associated with univariate age-related hyper-activation in other ROIs and tasks, leading to interpretations in terms of neural inefficiency rather than compensation.
source: This is the first demonstration of increased multivariate information with age, since previous studies have shown evidence for no such multivariate increase associated with univariate age-related hyper-activation in other ROIs and tasks; leading to previous findings being interpreted in terms of neural inefficiency, rather than compensation (Morcom and Henson, 2018; Knights et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings, supported by citations.

claim: The cuneus has a well-established role in visual attention.
source: Since the cuneus has a well-established role in visual attention (e.g., Corbetta et al., 1998), we hypothesise that the additional recruitment of this brain region facilitates concurrently attending to multiple features of the stimulus array, to correctly select the 'odd-one-out'.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The additional recruitment of the cuneus facilitates concurrently attending to multiple features of the stimulus array, to correctly select the 'odd-one-out'.
source: Since the cuneus has a well-established role in visual attention (e.g., Corbetta et al., 1998), we hypothesise that the additional recruitment of this brain region facilitates concurrently attending to multiple features of the stimulus array, to correctly select the 'odd-one-out'.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known role of the cuneus and the current findings.

claim: The recruitment of the cuneus in older adults could drive changes in looking strategy, where older adults compensate for their reduced visual short-term memory by using more or different saccades.
source: The recruitment of this brain region in older adults could drive changes in looking strategy (e.g., Law et al., 1996), where, for example, older adults compensate for their reduced visual short-term memory (Mitchell et al., 2018) – that is, difficulty sustaining representations of puzzle items – by using more or different saccades.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior work on looking strategies and visual short-term memory, supported by citations.

claim: The hypothesis about cuneal recruitment is consistent with the greater cuneal activation observed for older adults who performed better at the task.
source: This possibility is consistent with the greater cuneal activation that was observed for older adults who performed better at the task (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency between the hypothesis and the data, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: There is consistent functional and structural neuroimaging evidence that links the cuneal cortex to aspects of fluid intelligence like rule application.
source: In line with this hypothesised role of the cuneal cortex, there is consistent functional (Yin et al., 2015; Santarnecchi et al., 2017) and structural (Haier et al., 2004; Jauk et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2020) neuroimaging evidence that link this brain region to aspects of fluid intelligence like rule application.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior functional and structural neuroimaging studies.

claim: Responses from sensory areas (like the secondary visual network that overlaps the cuneus ROI) have been shown to predict fluid intelligence performance.
source: Similarly, responses from sensory areas (like the secondary visual network that overlaps our cuneus ROI; Ji et al., 2019) have been shown to predict fluid intelligence performance (Brumback et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In ageing, it is well established that sensory and intellectual decline are correlated.
source: In ageing, it is well established that sensory and intellectual decline are correlated (see Baltes and Lindenberger, 1997), either because they share a common cause or because performance of fluid intelligence tasks is partially dependent on sensory processing (e.g., Schneider and Pichora-Fuller, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Sensory and intellectual decline in ageing are correlated either because they share a common cause or because performance of fluid intelligence tasks is partially dependent on sensory processing.
source: In ageing, it is well established that sensory and intellectual decline are correlated (see Baltes and Lindenberger, 1997), either because they share a common cause or because performance of fluid intelligence tasks is partially dependent on sensory processing (e.g., Schneider and Pichora-Fuller, 2000).
evidence: This statement presents alternative explanations supported by citations.

claim: Compensatory processes in the cuneal region may reflect shared age-related variance between sensory and higher-order cognitive tasks.
source: While our data cannot tease apart these hypotheses, it may be that compensatory processes in the cuneal region reflect this shared age-related variance between sensory and higher-order cognitive tasks.
evidence: This is a speculation about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: The constant term for cuneal ROI activation was negative, suggesting that most people (other than the older ones) showed greater activation of this region for easy than hard problems.
source: Though activation of the cuneal ROI increased with age, it is worth noting the constant term (reflecting the average across all ages) was negative (Table 1), suggesting that most people (other than the older ones) showed greater activation of this region for easy than hard problems.
evidence: This is an observation from the statistical model in Table 1.

claim: Greater activation of the cuneus for easy than hard problems in the young is difficult to reconcile with its activation reflecting visual attention or eye movements.
source: This is more difficult to reconcile with its activation reflecting visual attention or eye movements, since this would suggest greater visual attention/eye movements towards easy than hard problems in the young.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: One alternative possibility is active suppression of the cuneal region in the hard blocks, to avoid distraction.
source: One alternative possibility is active suppression of the cuneal region in the hard blocks, to avoid distraction (e.g., minimise attentional capture from neighbouring display panels while processing features in each panel).
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis to explain the findings.

claim: The age-related reduction in the Easy − Hard difference could reflect reduced ability to inhibit the cuneus during hard problems, consistent with established age-related decline in the ability to suppress distracting information in complex stimuli.
source: Thus, the age-related reduction in the Easy − Hard difference (leading to the positive correlation of the Hard − Easy difference with age) could reflect reduced ability to inhibit the cuneus during hard problems, consistent with the established age-related decline in the ability to suppress distracting information in complex stimuli (Tsvetanov et al., 2013; Rey-Mermet and Gade, 2018; Bouhassoun et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis supported by citations to prior work on age-related decline in inhibition.

claim: It is not clear why the alternative account of reduced inhibition would predict a positive correlation between cuneal activity and task performance.
source: However, it is not clear why this alternative account would predict a positive correlation between cuneal activity and task performance, given that greater suppression (in the Hard condition) would be expected to lead to better performance, but more negative activity values for the [Hard − Easy] contrast.
evidence: This is a logical critique of the alternative hypothesis.

claim: The authors favour the explanation of cuneal activation in terms of functional compensation.
source: Thus, we favour the explanation in terms of functional compensation.
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' preferred interpretation.

claim: Another possibility is that the age-related increases in fMRI activations do not reflect greater fMRI signal for hard problems in older than younger people, but rather lower fMRI signal for easy problems in the older.
source: Another possibility is that the age-related increases in fMRI activations (for hard vs. easy) in one or both of our ROIs do not reflect greater fMRI signal for hard problems in older than younger people, but rather lower fMRI signal for easy problems in the older.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: Without a third baseline condition, the study cannot distinguish whether age-related increases reflect greater signal for hard or lower signal for easy problems.
source: Without a third baseline condition, we cannot distinguish these two possibilities in our data.
evidence: This is a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: A reduced 'baseline' level of fMRI signal for easy problems in older people is consistent with other studies showing an age-related decline in baseline perfusion levels, coupled with preserved capacity of cerebrovascular reactivity to meet metabolic demands of neuronal activity at higher cognitive load.
source: However, a reduced 'baseline' level of fMRI signal (e.g., for easy problems) in older people is consistent with other studies showing an age-related decline in baseline perfusion levels, coupled with preserved capacity of cerebrovascular reactivity to meet metabolic demands of neuronal activity at higher cognitive load (Calautti et al., 2001; Jennings et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on age-related changes in perfusion.

claim: Age-related decline in baseline perfusion occurs in the cuneal cortex.
source: Though age-related decline in baseline perfusion occurs in the cuneal cortex (Tsvetanov et al., 2021b), the brain regions showing modulation of behaviourally relevant Cattell fMRI activity by perfusion levels did not include the cuneal cortex (Wu et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The brain regions showing modulation of behaviourally relevant Cattell fMRI activity by perfusion levels did not include the cuneal cortex.
source: Though age-related decline in baseline perfusion occurs in the cuneal cortex (Tsvetanov et al., 2021b), the brain regions showing modulation of behaviourally relevant Cattell fMRI activity by perfusion levels did not include the cuneal cortex (Wu et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The compensatory effects in the cuneus are unlikely to be explained by age-related hypo-perfusion, consistent with the minimal effect of adjusting for RSFA.
source: This suggests that the compensatory effects in the cuneus are unlikely to be explained by age-related hypo-perfusion, consistent with the minimal effect here of adjusting for RSFA (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work and the RSFA-adjusted analysis, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: One possibility is whether the observed boost in decoding from adding the cuneal ROI simply reflects less noisy task-related information (i.e., a better SNR) than the MDN.
source: One final possibility is whether the observed boost in decoding from adding the cuneal ROI simply reflects less noisy task-related information (i.e., a better SNR) than the MDN and, consequently, the boosted decoding is the result of more resilient patterns of information (rather than the representation of additional information) based on a steeper age-related decline of SNR in the MDN.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis about the interpretation of the MVB findings.

claim: None of the alternative explanations agree with all aspects of the results.
source: Overall then, as none of the explanations above agree with all aspects of the results, to functionally explain the role of the cuneal cortex in this task would require further investigation.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the limitations of current interpretations.

claim: To functionally explain the role of the cuneal cortex in this task would require further investigation.
source: Overall then, as none of the explanations above agree with all aspects of the results, to functionally explain the role of the cuneal cortex in this task would require further investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research.

claim: The age- and performance-related activation in the frontal region satisfied the traditional univariate criteria for functional compensation.
source: The age- and performance-related activation in our frontal region satisfied the traditional univariate criteria for functional compensation, but our MVB model comparison analysis showed that additional multivariate information beyond that in the MDN was absent in this region, which is inconsistent with the strongest definition of compensation.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings for the frontal region.

claim: Additional multivariate information beyond that in the MDN was absent in the frontal region, which is inconsistent with the strongest definition of compensation.
source: The age- and performance-related activation in our frontal region satisfied the traditional univariate criteria for functional compensation, but our MVB model comparison analysis showed that additional multivariate information beyond that in the MDN was absent in this region, which is inconsistent with the strongest definition of compensation.
evidence: This is a summary of the MVB findings for the frontal region.

claim: As age increased, the frontal area processed less, rather than more, multivariate information about the cognitive outcome.
source: In fact, the results from the spread analysis showed that as age increased, this frontal area processed less, rather than more, multivariate information about the cognitive outcome (Figure 3C) as previously observed in two (memory) tasks for a comparable ROI within the same Cam-CAN cohort (Morcom and Henson, 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the MVB spread analysis with reference to Figure 3C and citation to prior work.

claim: Traditional univariate criteria alone are not sufficient for identifying functional compensation.
source: This pattern of results suggests that traditional univariate criteria alone are not sufficient for identifying functional compensation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of univariate and multivariate findings.

claim: Similar univariate effects have been found in previous studies, where lateral and medial frontal areas show increased activation during healthy ageing across a range of tasks.
source: Similar univariate effects have been found in previous studies (though with smaller samples), where lateral and medial frontal areas show increased activation during healthy ageing across a range of tasks, including those related to executive control or attention (e.g., Spreng et al., 2010; for a review, see Spreng et al., 2010; also see Raz et al., 2008, for a neuroanatomical link).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Patients with brain damage demonstrate increased frontal activation during language and semantic processing, indicating that this mechanism might be a response to brain atrophy generally.
source: Patients with brain damage also demonstrate increased frontal activation during language and semantic processing (Brownsett et al., 2014; Rice et al., 2018) indicating that this mechanism might be a response to brain atrophy generally.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies and includes an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Frontal hyper-activation in older adults reflects 'inefficient' processing, in terms of more neural resources being needed to perform the task.
source: Instead, our results suggest that this frontal hyper-activation in older adults reflects 'inefficient' processing, in terms of more neural resources being needed to perform the task (i.e., for hard vs. easy problems).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings for the frontal region.

claim: Neural inefficiency was the favoured interpretation of previous cases when MVB showed no age-related boost, in frontal or motor regions.
source: In fact, neural inefficiency was our favoured interpretation of previous cases when MVB showed no age-related boost, in frontal (Morcom and Henson, 2018) or motor (Knights et al., 2021) regions.
evidence: This statement refers to interpretations from prior studies by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: From previous fMRI or PET studies that showed age-related hyper-activation, it was not known whether the increased activations reflected greater neural inefficiency, or greater haemodynamic resources needed for the same level of neural activity.
source: From these studies, and all previous fMRI or positron emission tomography (PET) studies that showed age-related hyper-activation, it was not known whether the increased activations reflected greater neural inefficiency, or greater haemodynamic resources needed for the same level of neural activity (i.e., vascular rather than neural inefficiency).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior research.

claim: The study showed for the first time that the age-related increase in both ROIs remained even after adjusting for RSFA, suggesting that this hyper-activation reflects neural rather than vascular inefficiency.
source: Here, we showed for the first time that the age-related increase in both ROIs remained even after adjusting for RSFA (Table 1), suggesting that this hyper-activation reflects neural rather than vascular inefficiency.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the RSFA-adjusted analysis and its interpretation.

claim: Univariate criteria for functional compensation will continue to play a role in hypothesis testing.
source: This said, univariate criteria for functional compensation will continue to play a role in hypothesis testing.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of univariate approaches.

claim: The over-additive interaction observed in the cuneal cortex offers evidence of compensation compared to the simple additive effect observed in the frontal cortex.
source: For instance, the over-additive interaction observed in the cuneal cortex – where the increase in activity with better performance is more pronounced in older adults – offers evidence of compensation compared to the simple additive effect of age and performance observed in the frontal cortex (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the interaction pattern with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The conclusions that can be drawn from age-related differences in cross-sectional associations of brain and behaviour are limited, mainly because individual performance differences are largely lifespan-stable.
source: However, the conclusions that can be drawn from age-related differences in cross-sectional associations of brain and behaviour are limited, mainly because individual performance differences are largely lifespan-stable (see Lindenberger et al., 2011; Morcom and Johnson, 2015).
evidence: This is a limitation of cross-sectional designs, supported by citations.

claim: The two studies that have combined univariate, behavioural, and multivariate approaches to assess functional compensation have generally found converging evidence regardless of the method used.
source: So far, the two studies that have combined these univariate, behavioural, and multivariate approaches to assess functional compensation (i.e., Knights et al., 2021; the present study) have generally found converging evidence regardless of the method used.
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of findings across methods, with citation to prior work.

claim: The MVB approach uniquely shifts the focus from individual differences to the specific task-related information that compensatory neural activations are assumed to carry and provides a specific test of region-unique information.
source: However, it is important to note that the MVB approach uniquely shifts the focus from individual differences to the specific task-related information that compensatory neural activations are assumed to carry and provides a specific test of region- (or network-) unique information.
evidence: This is a statement about the unique contribution of the MVB approach.

claim: Multivariate approaches may prove more sensitive for detecting compensation effects than when using mean responses over voxels.
source: With further studies, it may also be that multivariate approaches prove more sensitive for detecting compensation effects than when using mean responses over voxels (e.g., Friston et al., 1995) particularly since over-additive effects are challenging to observe because compensatory effects are typically 'partial' and do not fully restore function (for review see Scheller et al., 2014; Morcom and Johnson, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential advantages of multivariate approaches, supported by citations.

claim: The stringent MVB boost likelihood analysis could detect functional compensation unlike the more lenient analysis focusing on the spread of MVB voxel weights.
source: Within the multivariate analysis options themselves, it is also interesting to highlight that the stringent MVB boost likelihood analysis could detect functional compensation unlike the more lenient analysis focusing on the spread of MVB voxel weights.
evidence: This is a comparison of the two MVB analysis approaches based on the current findings.

claim: The importance of including task-relevant network responses when building decoding models to assess compensation is highlighted.
source: This suggests the importance of including task-relevant network responses when building decoding models to assess compensation.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the findings.

claim: In Morcom and Henson, 2018, the authors did not explicitly test for a relationship between activation and memory performance.
source: In Morcom and Henson, 2018, we did not explicitly test for a relationship between activation and (memory) performance, and in Knights et al., 2021, we failed to find any relationship between (ipsilateral motor) activation and various (motor) performance measures.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work by the authors.

claim: In Knights et al., 2021, the authors failed to find any relationship between ipsilateral motor activation and various motor performance measures.
source: In Morcom and Henson, 2018, we did not explicitly test for a relationship between activation and (memory) performance, and in Knights et al., 2021, we failed to find any relationship between (ipsilateral motor) activation and various (motor) performance measures.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work by the authors.

claim: The age-related frontal hyper-activation may be caused by neural inefficiency, yet the degree of overall activation still relates to lifespan-stable problem-solving performance.
source: In the present study, it may be that the age-related frontal hyper-activation is caused by neural inefficiency, yet the degree of overall activation still relates to (lifespan-stable) problem-solving performance.
evidence: This is a speculation about the interpretation of the frontal findings.

claim: The lack of additional multivariate information in the frontal region suggests that it does not show a compensatory response.
source: Converging with the lack of additional multivariate information, this suggests that the frontal region does not show a compensatory response.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the MVB findings for the frontal region.

claim: The results in the cuneus represent the most compelling evidence to date for functional compensation in healthy ageing.
source: In summary, we propose that our results in the cuneus represent the most compelling evidence to date for functional compensation in healthy ageing, with further work needed to determine the precise function of this region in problem-solving tasks like that examined here.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the significance of the findings.

claim: Further work is needed to determine the precise function of the cuneus in problem-solving tasks.
source: In summary, we propose that our results in the cuneus represent the most compelling evidence to date for functional compensation in healthy ageing, with further work needed to determine the precise function of this region in problem-solving tasks like that examined here.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research.

claim: The data suggest that specific compensatory neural responses can coexist with inefficient neural function in older people.
source: Together with the results in prefrontal cortex, the data also suggest that specific compensatory neural responses can coexist with inefficient neural function in older people.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined findings for the cuneus and frontal regions.

claim: A healthy population-derived adult lifespan human sample (N = 223; ages approximately uniformly distributed from 19 to 87 years; females = 112; 50.2%) was collected as part of the Cam-CAN study.
source: A healthy population-derived adult lifespan human sample (N = 223; ages approximately uniformly distributed from 19 to 87 years; females = 112; 50.2%) was collected as part of the Cam-CAN study (Stage 3 cohort; Shafto et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: Participants were fluent English speakers in good physical and mental health, based on the Cam-CAN cohort's exclusion criteria.
source: Participants were fluent English speakers in good physical and mental health, based on the Cam-CAN cohort's exclusion criteria which includes poor mini mental state examination, ineligibility for MRI and medical, psychiatric, hearing, or visual problems.
evidence: This describes the participant inclusion/exclusion criteria.

claim: The study was approved by the Cambridgeshire 2 (now East of England – Cambridge Central) Research Ethics Committee (reference: 10/H0308/50).
source: The study was approved by the Cambridgeshire 2 (now East of England – Cambridge Central) Research Ethics Committee (reference: 10/H0308/50) and participants provided informed written consent.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Participants provided informed written consent.
source: The study was approved by the Cambridgeshire 2 (now East of England – Cambridge Central) Research Ethics Committee (reference: 10/H0308/50) and participants provided informed written consent.
evidence: This describes the consent process.

claim: A modified version of the odd-one-out subtest of the standardised Cattell Culture Fair Intelligence test (Scale 2) was developed for use in the scanner.
source: A modified version of the odd-one-out subtest of the standardised Cattell Culture Fair Intelligence test (Scale 2; Cattell, 1971; Cattell and Cattell, 1973) was developed for use in the scanner (Woolgar et al., 2013; Samu et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2023).
evidence: This describes the task used in the study, with citations to the original test and prior uses.

claim: Participants were scanned while performing the problem-solving task where, on each trial, four display panels were presented in a horizontal row in the centre of a screen viewed through a head-coil mounted mirror.
source: Participants were scanned while performing the problem-solving task where, on each trial, four display panels were presented in a horizontal row (Figure 1A) in the centre of a screen that was viewed through a head-coil mounted mirror.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Participants were required to make a button-press response to identify the mismatching panel that was unique in some way from the other three.
source: Participants were required to make a button-press response to identify the mismatching panel that was unique in some way from the other three (based on either a figural, spatial, complex, or abstract property).
evidence: This describes the task requirements.

claim: Participants completed eight 30-s blocks which contained a series of puzzles from one of two difficulty levels (four hard and four easy blocks completed in an alternating block order).
source: In a block design, participants completed eight 30-s blocks which contained a series of puzzles from one of two difficulty levels (i.e., four hard and four easy blocks completed in an alternating block order; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Behavioural performance was measured by subtracting the number of incorrect from correct trials and averaging over the hard and easy blocks independently.
source: Therefore, to balance speed and accuracy, behavioural performance was measured by subtracting the number of incorrect from correct trials and averaging over the hard and easy blocks independently (i.e., ((hard correct − hard incorrect) + (easy correct − easy incorrect))/2; Samu et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the performance measure with citation to prior work.

claim: The study excluded participants (N = 28; 17 females) who performed at chance level ((correct + incorrect)/incorrect <0.5) on the fMRI task.
source: We excluded participants (N = 28; 17 females) who performed at chance level ((correct + incorrect)/incorrect <0.5) on the fMRI task, leading to the same subset as reported in Samu et al., 2017.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria with citation to prior work.

claim: The MRI data were collected using a Siemens 3T TIM TRIO system with a 32-channel head-coil.
source: The MRI data were collected using a Siemens 3T TIM TRIO system with a 32-channel head-coil.
evidence: This describes the MRI scanner used.

claim: A T2*-weighted echoplanar imaging sequence was used to collect 150 volumes, each containing 32 axial slices acquired in descending order.
source: A T2*-weighted echoplanar imaging sequence was used to collect 150 volumes, each containing 32 axial slices (acquired in descending order) with slice thickness of 3.0 mm and an interslice gap of 25% for whole-brain coverage (repetition time, RT = 2000 ms; echo time, TE = 30 ms; flip angle = 78°; field of view, FOV = 192 mm × 192 mm; voxel-size 3 × 3 × 3.75 mm).
evidence: This describes the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Higher resolution (1 mm × 1 mm × 1 mm) T1- and T2-weighted structural images were also acquired to aid registration across participants.
source: Higher resolution (1 mm × 1 mm × 1 mm) T1- and T2-weighted structural images were also acquired (to aid registration across participants).
evidence: This describes the structural imaging acquisition.

claim: MR data pre-processing and univariate analysis were performed with SPM12 software, release 4537, implemented in the AA 4.0 pipeline.
source: MR data pre-processing and univariate analysis were performed with SPM12 software (Wellcome Department of Imaging Neuroscience, London, https://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/), release 4537, implemented in the AA 4.0 pipeline (Cusack et al., 2014) described in Taylor et al., 2017.
evidence: This describes the software and pipeline used for analysis, with citations.

claim: All ROIs were defined by selecting activated voxels from a group-level GLM.
source: All ROIs were defined by selecting activated voxels from a group-level GLM (see Table 2 for number of voxels within ROIs).
evidence: This describes the ROI definition method.

claim: The two ROIs tested as candidate regions for functional compensation (cuneal cortex and frontal cortex) were defined by contiguous voxels that were significantly positively related to the independent effects of both age and performance.
source: The two ROIs that were tested as candidate regions for functional compensation (i.e., cuneal cortex and frontal cortex) were defined by contiguous voxels that were significantly positively related to the independent effects of both age and performance (see Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the ROI definition method with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The MDN was defined by selecting suprathreshold voxels activated by the [Hard vs. Easy] contrast from the Cattell task.
source: The MDN was defined by the selecting suprathreshold voxels activated by the [Hard vs. Easy] contrast from the Cattell task.
evidence: This describes the MDN ROI definition method.

claim: For MVB analysis, a subset of the highest activated voxels within the MDN were taken to match the number of voxels with that of the 'compensation ROI' being tested.
source: For MVB analysis (see below), a subset of the highest activated voxels within the MDN were taken to match the number of voxels with that of the 'compensation ROI' being tested (see Figure 3; Table 2).
evidence: This describes the voxel selection for MVB analysis with reference to Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: Each MVB decoding model is based on the same design matrix of experimental variables used in the univariate GLM, but the mapping is reversed.
source: Each MVB decoding model is based on the same design matrix of experimental variables used in the univariate GLM, but the mapping is reversed; many physiological data features (fMRI activity in multiple voxels) are used to predict a psychological target variable (Friston et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the MVB method with citation.

claim: The target (outcome) variable in MVB is specified as the contrast [Hard > Easy] with all covariates removed from the predictor variables.
source: This target (outcome) variable is specified as the contrast [Hard > Easy] with all covariates removed from the predictor variables.
evidence: This describes the MVB target variable.

claim: Each MVB model was fit using a parametric empirical Bayes approach, in which empirical priors on the data features are specified in terms of spatial patterns over voxel features and the variances of the pattern weights.
source: Each MVB model was fit using a parametric empirical Bayes approach, in which empirical priors on the data features (voxel-wise activity) are specified in terms of spatial patterns over voxel features and the variances of the pattern weights.
evidence: This describes the MVB fitting method.

claim: A sparse spatial prior in which 'patterns' are individual voxels was used in MVB.
source: As in earlier work (Morcom and Henson, 2018; Knights et al., 2021), we used a sparse spatial prior in which 'patterns' are individual voxels.
evidence: This describes the MVB prior specification with citations to prior work.

claim: The pattern weights specifying the mapping of data features to the target variable are optimised with a greedy search algorithm using a standard variational scheme.
source: The pattern weights specifying the mapping of data features to the target variable are optimised with a greedy search algorithm using a standard variational scheme (Friston et al., 2008) which was particularly appropriate given the large dataset.
evidence: This describes the MVB optimization method with citation.

claim: The free energy provides an upper bound on the log of the Bayesian model evidence.
source: This is achieved by maximising the free energy, which provides an upper bound on the log of the Bayesian model evidence (the marginal probability of the data given that model).
evidence: This describes a property of the MVB method.

claim: The evidence for different models predicting the same psychological variable can be compared by computing the difference in log evidences, which is equivalent to the log of the Bayes factor.
source: The evidence for different models predicting the same psychological variable can then be compared by computing the difference in log evidences, which is equivalent to the log of the Bayes factor (Friston et al., 2008; Chadwick et al., 2012; Morcom and Friston, 2012).
evidence: This describes the MVB model comparison method with citations.

claim: The outcome measure in MVB was the log evidence for each model.
source: The outcome measure was the log evidence for each model (Morcom and Henson, 2018; Knights et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the MVB outcome measure with citations to prior work.

claim: An ordinal boost measure was used to assess the contribution of an ROI for the decoding of task-relevant information.
source: To test whether activity from an ROI is compensatory, we used an ordinal boost measure (Morcom and Henson, 2018; Knights et al., 2021) to assess the contribution of that ROI for the decoding of task-relevant information (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the MVB boost measure with citations to prior work and reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Bayesian model comparison assessed whether a model that contains activity patterns from a compensatory ROI and the MDN (a joint model) boosted the prediction of task-relevant information relative to a model containing the MDN only.
source: Specifically, Bayesian model comparison assessed whether a model that contains activity patterns from a compensatory ROI and the MDN (i.e., a joint model) boosted the prediction of task-relevant information relative to a model containing the MDN only.
evidence: This describes the MVB model comparison approach.

claim: The compensatory hypothesis predicts that the likelihood of a boost to model decoding will increase with older age.
source: The compensatory hypothesis predicts that the likelihood of a boost to model decoding will increase with older age.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the compensation hypothesis.

claim: The dependent measure for each participant was a categorical recoding of the relative model evidence to indicate the outcome of the model comparison.
source: The dependent measure, for each participant, was a categorical recoding of the relative model evidence to indicate the outcome of the model comparison.
evidence: This describes the dependent variable for the boost analysis.

claim: The three possible outcomes of the model comparison were: a boost to model evidence for the joint vs. MDN-only model (difference in log evidence >3), ambiguous evidence for the two models (difference in log evidence between −3 and 3), or a reduction in evidence for the joint vs. MDN-only model (difference in log evidence <−3).
source: The three possible outcomes were: a boost to model evidence for the joint vs. MDN-only model (difference in log evidence >3), ambiguous evidence for the two models (difference in log evidence between −3 and 3), or a reduction in evidence for the joint vs. MDN-only model (difference in log evidence <−3).
evidence: This describes the categorization of model comparison outcomes.

claim: A log difference of three corresponds to a Bayes factor of 20, which is generally considered strong evidence.
source: These values were selected because a log difference of three corresponds to a Bayes factor of 20, which is generally considered strong evidence (Lee and Wagenmakers, 2014).
evidence: This is a justification for the threshold used, with citation.

claim: With uniform priors, the chosen criterion of log difference of three corresponds to a p-value of <~0.05.
source: Furthermore, with uniform priors, this chosen criterion corresponds to a p-value of <~0.05 (since the natural logarithm of 20 equals three, as evidence for the alternative hypothesis).
evidence: This is a justification for the threshold used based on statistical reasoning.

claim: A reduction in model evidence was not observed in the current study.
source: A reduction in model evidence was not observed in the current study.
evidence: This is a finding from the MVB boost analysis.

claim: For the MVB boost analysis, participants were only included if their data allowed reliable decoding by the joint model.
source: For this MVB boost analysis, participants were only included if their data allowed reliable decoding by the joint model (Morcom and Henson, 2018; Knights et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the MVB boost analysis with citations to prior work.

claim: Reliable decoding was defined based on a mean of 3 or more in the difference of log evidence between the true and shuffled model.
source: The definition of reliable was based on a mean of 3 or more in the difference of log evidence between the true and shuffled model (Morcom and Henson, 2018; Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the reliability criterion with citation to prior work and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: MVB decoding is performed after removing the mean across voxels, making MVB results independent of the univariate analyses.
source: Note that decoding is performed after removing the mean across voxels (i.e., MVB results are independent of the results in the univariate analyses presented in Figure 1C and Table 1).
evidence: This describes a property of the MVB method.

claim: The spread (standard deviation) of voxel classification weights indexes the absolute amplitude of voxel contributions to the task, reflecting the degree to which multiple voxels carry substantial task-related information.
source: Alongside the MVB boost analysis, we also included an additional measure using the spread (standard deviation) of voxel classification weights (Morcom and Henson, 2018). This measure indexes the absolute amplitude of voxel contributions to the task, reflecting the degree to which multiple voxels carry substantial task-related information.
evidence: This describes the MVB spread measure with citation to prior work.

claim: When the spread measure is related to age, it can serve as a multivariate index of information distribution, unlike univariate analyses.
source: When related to age this can serve as a multivariate index of information distribution, unlike univariate analyses.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the spread measure.

claim: The MVB boost analysis is the most compelling assessment of functional compensation because it can directly detect novel information representation.
source: Thus, it is the MVB boost analysis that is the most compelling assessment of functional compensation because it can directly detect novel information representation.
evidence: This is a statement about the relative value of the MVB boost analysis.

claim: Continuous age and behavioural performance variables were standardised and treated as linear predictors in multiple regression throughout the analyses.
source: Continuous age and behavioural performance variables were standardised and treated as linear predictors in multiple regression throughout the behavioural (Figure 1B), wholebrain voxel-wise (Figures 1C and 2A), univariate (Table 1; Figures 1B and 2B), and MVB (Table 2; Figure 3) analyses.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used throughout the study.

claim: Sex was included as a covariate throughout the analyses.
source: Throughout, sex was included as a covariate.
evidence: This describes a covariate included in the statistical models.

claim: For whole-brain voxel-wise analyses, clusters were estimated using threshold-free cluster enhancement with 2000 permutations.
source: For whole-brain voxel-wise analyses, clusters were estimated using threshold-free cluster enhancement (Smith and Nichols, 2009) with 2000 permutations and the resulting images were thresholded at a t-statistic of 1.97 before interpretation.
evidence: This describes the statistical method for whole-brain analysis with citation.

claim: Bonferroni correction was applied to a standard alpha = 0.05 based on the two ROIs (cuneal and frontal) that were examined.
source: Bonferroni correction was applied to a standard alpha = 0.05 based on the two ROIs (cuneal and frontal) that were examined.
evidence: This describes the multiple comparison correction applied.
